title: Grading and Road Construction
body: A high spot or a badly graded switchback doesn't just look untidy — it cracks tires, throws payload unevenly across the tray, and turns a routine ramp turn into where trucks lose traction and visibility. At ADW that's already shown up as real cost: the tire/suspension escalation this cycle is partly a road-condition problem, not just a tire problem.
keyPoints: High spots and switchbacks are the two things a daily pit inspection should always be checking for — a raised area needs the grader now, not next shift, because it compounds with every pass.

Switchbacks need more than a flat pass: super-elevation (banking), inside-radius clearance, and outside bund integrity all matter there specifically, because that's where trucks lose visibility and traction and where most ramp incidents happen.
Grade in the direction of traffic flow, diff lock on, no sharp turns with diff lock engaged, and grade spillage to the side — basic operator discipline that gets skipped when a grader's rushed.

Grading alone can't fix a base-material problem. If a road is hard-packed and won't compact right, patching with soft/sand material (or crusher screening) into the surface is the actual fix — regrading a road that's fundamentally too hard just wastes a pass.
No unsupervised grading within the 10 m high-wall no-go zone — the high-wall exclusion rule always overrides the grading routine.
apply: If a switchback feels loose or trucks are cutting the inside radius on any ramp today, that's a grading and bund-integrity issue, not a driver issue — get it flagged for the grader before it turns into a near-miss.
